title: CBA records slump in home loan requests
full_text:
Australia’s biggest bank has reported a collapse in home loan application volumes since Labor announced major property tax changes in the May budget, but it has played down the impact of price falls.
The slide in applications from both investors and owner occupiers prompted the country’s chief real estate lobby to call on state governments, whose stamp duty revenues have been smashed, to urge a rethink by Jim Chalmers on the tax changes at a national treasurers meeting to be held this week.
Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn reported a 28 per cent collapse in investor loan application volumes since May. The bank, which is the country’s biggest residential lender, also reported a 9 per cent slide in owner-occupier lending application volumes since that time.
It also noted that of all the home loans it struck in 2023, almost 2 per cent were now more than 30 days in arrears.
The data follows Westpac revealing this week that investor loan applications had fallen by 30 per cent. ANZ is expected to report similar numbers at its update on Thursday.
While the collapse in applications is a concern, Mr Comyn raced to calm the market, saying applications had stabilised in the past few weeks and that he was not concerned about forecasts for a 5 to 10 per cent property price correction, given the run-up in house prices in the past few years.
“If housing were to fall by sort of 5 per cent it goes back to where prices were at a national level in August 2025, and a 10 per cent (fall) takes us back to sort of January 2025. So, I’m not suggesting it’s not an important issue (but) I don’t think it’s as important as longer-term productivity,” Mr Comyn said.
“I think there is volatility. You can see there’s an increase in arrears in housing,” he said.
After Westpac this week revealed a similar slide in home loan applications, Westpac CEO Anthony Miller said budget hits on negative gearing and capital gains tax discounts had driven “uncertainty” as Australians seek to “navigate that new regime”.
Amid concerns over declining property prices and first homebuyers being impacted by negative equity, Mr Miller discussed a new reality in which Australians may need to accept home values might not improve “as steeply as we’ve seen in terms of price increases in the past”.
Mr Miller also linked a stronger property market with the wealth effect and people’s desire to “spend money, go on holidays, and do things that drive the economy”.
He said not many Australians in recent decades have had to feel that “their property is worth less than what they purchased”.
“That’s something that not many people have endured and so it is something that we do worry about, which is what does that mean for that person at a very human level? Does that mean they’re a little less confident now in their next action? Will they spend a little less? Are they a little bit more worried? Is the quality of their life impacted?
“Because I think many people, and it’s a fair assumption, have assumed that if you buy a property over time you’ll see it improve in value. And I think that remains correct, that you will see your house value improve over time. It just may not be as steep as we’ve seen in terms of price increases in the past.”
As prices fall, so do stamp duties, with an estimated $7bn to be swiped off state budget revenues. On Wednesday, the country’s chief real estate lobby – Property Council of Australia chief executive Mike Zorbas – issued a challenge to state treasurers to convince the federal government it had gone too far and got the timing wrong on property tax changes.
“I hope the state treasurers get a clear answer from Treasurer Chalmers about who is going to pay for this anti-aspiration red tape and their falling stamp duty revenues when they meet up tomorrow at the Council on Federal Financial Relations,” he said.
‘The Reserve Bank governor is dead right to say the housing slump is a surprise caused by rates and “recent policy developments”.
“The May federal budget tax hikes have battered market confidence and right now are shrinking the new supply of housing, industrial and commercial projects across the country.”
He said national markets were eerily quiet over the past month and that the “confidence vacuum hurts new supply and comes before the upcoming double taxation of discretionary trusts is added on top of capital gains tax, negative gearing and SMSF changes”.
